awd_titl_txt: Workshop: Collaborative Research: NSF/M3X Visioning Workshop on Formalization of Human Factors into Computational Models; New York, New York; September 2025
awd_abstract_narration:
This grant supports a workshop on the formalization of human factors into computational models. The workshop will convene 40 participants with expertise in human factors, behavioral economics, cognitive neuroscience, social psychology, human-centered design, control theory, robotics, formal methods, and autonomous systems. Through presentations and discussions, participants will articulate the state-of-the-art capabilities in these fields while identifying research gaps and challenges related to the development and implementation of theoretical and computational models of human factors. An interdisciplinary approach that facilitates a common language and objectives across disciplines is key to this endeavor. The results of this workshop will advance the fields of robotics, dynamics, and control by identifying advanced capabilities and technologies that could arise from the use of models that methodologically capture non-trivial human behaviors. The results of this workshop will help advance the science of autonomous systems and could broadly impact research directions and capabilities in robotics and control. After the workshop, a report will be generated to summarize the findings, which will be shared with the general research community.

Despite extensive work in the development of autonomous dynamical systems, system capabilities are fundamentally limited by the challenges associated with effective, accurate, and computationally tractable models of human factors. To move the field beyond simplistic assumptions of human behavior that limit system capabilities, new approaches are needed to more faithfully capture the complexities humans bring to autonomous systems. The activities of this workshop are designed to bring together systems and controls researchers who share the challenge of translating important concepts from behavioral economics, social psychology, human factors, and human-centered design into frameworks amenable to computation and control of dynamical systems. Workshop activities will help participants develop and employ a common language that facilitates a meaningful exchange of ideas across disciplines to articulate better a roadmap for addressing research gaps and challenges that exist in formalizing human factors into computational models. Identifying these challenges is essential for advancing the field of systems and control.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This award supported an interdisciplinary visioning workshop, "Formalization of Human Factors into Computational Models," held September 18–19, 2025, in Alexandria, VA. The workshop's goal was to identify the gaps in our scientific understanding of how humans interact with autonomous, engineered systems, such as the self-driving cars, surgical robots, aircraft automation, and other AI-driven systems increasingly operating in the world around us, and to articulate a vision for what research in this area would significantly advance the field.

Autonomous systems, despite the name, inevitably require people.  While it is tempting to assume that autonomous systems can simply replace human function and decision making, a long history of incidents and accidents involving confusion, mistrust, and outright conflict between humans and automation demonstrate that it is important to design autonomous systems with interaction with humans in mind.  As artificial intelligence takes on more sophisticated tasks and greater responsibility for decision-making, these problems will only become more pervasive.  Hence it is important to better understand how humans and AI-driven systems can and should interact.

The workshop brought together 34 researchers and 4 organizers from 26 institutions, spanning academia, industry (including Raytheon and Toyota Research Institute), and government labs (including NASA, the Air Force Research Laboratory, and the Naval Research Laboratory). Crucially, the workshop united researchers who rarely interact directly: control theory, robotics, and formal methods experts who build autonomous systems, discussed with human factors, cognitive science, and social psychology experts who study human behavior itself. Two graduate students helped lead the workshop's day-to-day activities.  The event also included a dedicated question-and-answer session with five NSF Program Directors, connecting the research community's needs directly to the agency shaping the field's future.

The workshop produced several key outcomes:

  • Strong, shared agreement across disciplines regarding the need to address this problem together, rather than within any single field.

  • A fresh framing of a long-standing challenge in light of today's rapidly advancing, increasingly autonomous, AI-enabled systems.

  • Identification of common goals, methods, tools, datasets, and funding mechanisms that are required to advance the field as a coordinated community rather than as isolated research groups.

  • An articulation of application areas, such as aerospace systems, biomedical devices, intelligent transportation systems, and robotics, for which better models of human behavior are essential to making AI-driven systems safe, effective, and acceptable to operate in and around people.

Participants repeatedly noted that this kind of cross-disciplinary exchange is both important and rare, and that researchers in these fields often lack support for this work within their home disciplines and conferences.  This workshop began forming more robust connections between those communities.

The workshop's success directly motivated a follow-on proposal for a Research Coordination Network, Computational Human-AI Interaction Models for Engineered Systems (CHIMES), designed to sustain this community for years to come through annual research retreats, graduate student training practicums, cross-institutional student exchanges, and a shared repository of human-AI interaction data. A post-workshop survey of 55 invitees and participants found that 98% wanted to continue to participate in this kind of ongoing network, demonstrating the clear demand for this kind of community. The organizing team is also coordinating additional themed workshops for human factors, controls, robotics, and social science communities individually, to continue spreading the challenges and goals identified at this workshop to the broader research community.  Ultimately, this work aims to make AI-driven systems safer and more trustworthy as they take on greater roles in daily life, by embedding findings from social and behavioral sciences into engineering design.
